title: WebRTC and SIP over WebSocket
summary: How a browser reaches SIP: RFC 7118 on the signaling socket, ICE for candidates, and DTLS-SRTP for the media.

lessons.title: Signaling, JSEP, and the media plane
lessons.summary: WebRTC names a browser protocol suite. JSEP leaves the signaling protocol to the application. SIP over WebSocket is one such protocol.
objectives: Separate the browser media stack from the signaling protocol
Say what RFC 8825 and RFC 8829 each are
Name RFC 7118 as SIP on a WebSocket, not a new SIP method

illustration.title: Three jobs, three documents
illustration.caption: The application chooses signaling. The browser still has to carry media the WebRTC suite names.

layers.name: Application signaling
layers.detail: SIP over WebSocket is RFC 7118. JSEP also allows something custom.

layers.name: Session description
layers.detail: JSEP passes local and remote descriptions through the browser API.

layers.name: Media
layers.detail: RTP in the WebRTC context is RFC 8834. ICE is a separate traversal protocol.

sections.h: WebRTC is a suite, not a SIP method
paragraphs: RFC 8825 is an applicability statement for real-time communication in browsers. It does not itself specify a protocol. It points at the other specifications an implementation follows to be compliant with WebRTC.

RFC 8829, the JavaScript Session Establishment Protocol, says the browser API should control the signaling state while the JavaScript chooses the signaling protocol. The document names the existing SIP call signaling protocol as one option, and a custom protocol as another. The object that has to move is the session description.

sections.h: SIP over WebSocket is still SIP
paragraphs: RFC 7118 specifies a WebSocket subprotocol so SIP requests and responses can cross a WebSocket connection. It is a transport document. It does not replace INVITE, REGISTER, or the status codes.

RFC 6455 is the WebSocket protocol under that subprotocol: an opening handshake, then message framing over TCP. A browser softphone that uses SIP is combining that transport with ordinary SIP methods, then a media stack that is specified elsewhere.

lessons.title: RFC 7118: the sip subprotocol
lessons.summary: The handshake must offer sip. Via uses WS or WSS. The URI transport parameter added by the RFC is ws.
objectives: Tell Via WSS from a Contact transport=ws
Say why a browser example uses a .invalid host

illustration.title: Tokens from RFC 7118
illustration.caption: These are the names the RFC adds. They are not new SIP methods.
rows: Client and 101 reply both carry this subprotocol
The transport parameter the RFC adds
Service value for a SIP WebSocket server

paragraphs: During the WebSocket opening handshake, the client must include the value sip in Sec-WebSocket-Protocol. The 101 response must include sip as well. IANA registered that subprotocol identifier as sip, with the common name WebSocket Transport for SIP.

Section 5.4 of RFC 7118 quotes the RFC 3261 rule that SIP elements must implement UDP and TCP, then states the exception this transport exists for: a SIP element acting as a SIP WebSocket client is not mandated to implement UDP and TCP. A browser stack can be SIP without opening port 5060.

sections.h: Via, Contact, and the certificate check
paragraphs: Via uses WS on a plain WebSocket and WSS when the WebSocket connection was opened with TLS. The URI transport parameter the RFC adds is transport=ws. The registration example in section 8 uses transport=ws on Contact even while Via says WSS, and it uses a random .invalid host because that example's browser stack cannot learn the local address of the connection.

Section 9 recommends a secure WebSocket. The client must authenticate the server using the WebSocket validation procedure in RFC 6455. The RFC says that procedure differs from the SIP domain certificate procedure in RFC 5922. If a sips path includes a WebSocket hop, that hop must be a secure WebSocket. Keepalives may be WebSocket Ping frames. The RFC notes that the browser WebSocket API does not give the page a control for those Pings, and that the CRLF keepalives in RFC 5626 and RFC 6223 can still be used.

lessons.title: ICE, STUN, and TURN
lessons.summary: ICE gathers host, server-reflexive, and relayed candidates. STUN and TURN are the tools. The default STUN port is 3478.
objectives: Name the three candidate kinds in RFC 8445
Give the default STUN ports from RFC 8489
Say what a TURN relay adds

illustration.title: Numbers and roles
illustration.caption: Ports are the defaults in RFC 8489. Candidate names are from RFC 8445.
rows: Address on the public side of a NAT

sections.h: ICE tries pairs until one works
paragraphs: RFC 8445 describes ICE for UDP NAT traversal. It uses STUN and TURN. It obsoletes RFC 5245. A host candidate is taken from a local interface. STUN or TURN then adds server-reflexive candidates, the translated address on the public side of a NAT, and relayed candidates, the address on a TURN server.

If the agent uses only a STUN server, it gets server-reflexive candidates. Relayed candidates come from a TURN server. RFC 8839 specifies the SDP offer/answer procedures for carrying out ICE between the agents. The signaling protocol that carries that SDP can be SIP. ICE itself is not a SIP method.

RFC 8489 says the default port for STUN requests is 3478, for both TCP and UDP. The default port for STUN over TLS and STUN over DTLS is 5349. STUN lets an endpoint learn the mapped address allocated by a NAT. It is a tool other protocols use.

RFC 8656 defines TURN, a relay extension of STUN. The client controls the relay and exchanges packets with peers through it. One relay address can serve multiple peers. TURN was designed for use with ICE and can also be used without ICE. A relay is the path when a direct candidate pair does not work. It is not a substitute for the SIP dialog.

lessons.title: DTLS-SRTP and the required audio codecs
lessons.summary: WebRTC media is SRTP. The profile is RTP/SAVPF. Opus, PCMA, and PCMU are required audio codecs.
objectives: Say where DTLS-SRTP keys are made
Write the UDP proto token from RFC 5764

illustration.title: Keys on the media path
illustration.caption: DTLS-SRTP does not put the SRTP key in the SIP message. The codec list is a separate requirement.

layers.name: SIP
layers.detail: Agrees the session and can carry SDP

layers.name: DTLS
layers.detail: Handshake on the media path. use_srtp is the extension.

layers.name: SRTP
layers.detail: Protects RTP and RTCP. Profile RTP/SAVPF for WebRTC.

layers.name: Codecs
layers.detail: Opus, PCMA, and PCMU are required. Opus rtpmap clock is 48000, channels 2.

sections.h: DTLS keys the media, not the SIP hop
paragraphs: RFC 5764 describes a DTLS extension to establish keys for SRTP and SRTCP. The abstract says DTLS keying happens on the media path, independent of any out-of-band signaling channel. The extension type named in the RFC is use_srtp (14), and it must be used with DTLS, not with TLS.

When RTP/SAVPF is transported over DTLS with UDP, RFC 5764 says the SDP proto token shall be UDP/TLS/RTP/SAVPF. RFC 8834 requires WebRTC endpoints to implement RTP/SAVPF, the combination of RTP/AVP, RTP/AVPF, and RTP/SAVP. Those endpoints must not send with the basic RTP/AVP or RTP/AVPF profile. They must use SRTP and SRTCP. RFC 8834 says the RTP/SAVPF profile must be configured with the cipher suites, DTLS-SRTP protection profiles, and keying mechanisms described in RFC 8827. RFC 8827 treats a WebRTC peer authenticated via DTLS-SRTP as one of the authenticated-entity classes.

RFC 7874 requires WebRTC endpoints to implement Opus, with the payload format in RFC 7587, and PCMA and PCMU as specified in G.711 with the payload format in RFC 3551. It also requires comfort noise from RFC 3389 for G.711 or any other supported codec that does not provide its own comfort noise. Opus provides its own comfort noise, and RFC 7874 says using RFC 3389 comfort noise with Opus is not recommended.

RFC 7587 says the media subtype opus goes in a=rtpmap, the RTP clock rate must be 48000, and the number of channels must be 2. An example in that RFC is a=rtpmap:101 opus/48000/2. The payload type number can change. The encoding name, clock, and channel count are the match. Offering other codecs is recommended by RFC 7874 when they are available, so the session can avoid transcoding.

lessons.summary: A study ladder: WebSocket handshake, SIP INVITE, answer, then DTLS on the media path. Step the hops.
objectives: Order the handshake before the INVITE
Keep DTLS off the SIP transaction
Use the step control to read one hop at a time

illustration.title: Order that matches the documents
illustration.caption: Select a hop in the interactive flow. Each caption is a study note, not a packet captured from a vendor.

states.name: 2. INVITE
states.detail: SIP on that socket, SDP in the body

states.name: 4. DTLS
states.detail: Media path, after the description is known

paragraphs: The interactive flow on this page is a synthetic call. Addresses are from the documentation ranges in RFC 5737. The phone number uses 555. Nothing here was captured from a carrier.

The first hop is the WebSocket handshake from RFC 6455 with the sip subprotocol from RFC 7118. INVITE, 100, 180, 200, and ACK are SIP on that connection. The DTLS hop is last because RFC 5764 keys SRTP on the media path after the peers know where to send media. Stepping backward and treating DTLS as a SIP response will not match either document.

sections.h: What this ladder does not prove
paragraphs: RFC 8829 allows SIP or a custom signaling protocol. This ladder shows the SIP choice. A page that uses a custom protocol would still exchange a session description and would still run ICE and DTLS-SRTP if it is a WebRTC endpoint.

A gateway toward a trunk that is not a WebRTC endpoint is an application problem, not a status code in RFC 7118. This lab does not invent that gateway's configuration. If the far side cannot do DTLS-SRTP, the failure belongs in the media description and the DTLS handshake, which you can see by stepping to those hops.

steps.label: GET
steps.note: Handshake. Ask for subprotocol sip.
steps.message:
GET /sip HTTP/1.1
Host: proxy.example.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: sip
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13

steps.note: Server accepts sip. The WebSocket is open.
steps.message:
HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: sip

steps.label: INVITE
steps.note: SIP INVITE on the socket. SDP offers UDP/TLS/RTP/SAVPF and Opus, PCMU, and PCMA.
steps.message:
INVITE sip:+15551212@203.0.113.20 SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/WSS labua.invalid;branch=z9hG4bKlabws02
Max-Forwards: 70
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=labws2
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>
Call-ID: lab-ws-call@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Contact: <sip:alice@labua.invalid;transport=ws>
Content-Type: application/sdp
Content-Length: 187

v=0
o=browser 1 1 IN IP4 203.0.113.10
s=-
c=IN IP4 203.0.113.10
t=0 0
m=audio 49170 UDP/TLS/RTP/SAVPF 111 0 8
a=rtpmap:111 opus/48000/2
a=rtpmap:0 PCMU/8000
a=rtpmap:8 PCMA/8000

steps.note: Hop-by-hop Trying. Not the media handshake.
steps.message:
SIP/2.0 100 Trying
Via: SIP/2.0/WSS labua.invalid;branch=z9hG4bKlabws02
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=labws2
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>
Call-ID: lab-ws-call@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Content-Length: 0

steps.note: Alerting. Still no DTLS.
steps.message:
SIP/2.0 180 Ringing
Via: SIP/2.0/WSS labua.invalid;branch=z9hG4bKlabws02
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=labws2
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>;tag=gw180
Call-ID: lab-ws-call@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Contact: <sip:gw@203.0.113.20>
Content-Length: 0

steps.note: Answer SDP. The dialog can be confirmed. Media protection is still DTLS-SRTP.
steps.message:
SIP/2.0 200 OK
Via: SIP/2.0/WSS labua.invalid;branch=z9hG4bKlabws02
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=labws2
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>;tag=gw180
Call-ID: lab-ws-call@example.com
CSeq: 1 INVITE
Contact: <sip:gw@203.0.113.20>
Content-Type: application/sdp
Content-Length: 139

v=0
o=gateway 2 1 IN IP4 203.0.113.20
s=-
c=IN IP4 203.0.113.20
t=0 0
m=audio 19642 UDP/TLS/RTP/SAVPF 111
a=rtpmap:111 opus/48000/2

steps.label: ACK
steps.note: ACK confirms the 200. It does not carry the SRTP key.
steps.message:
ACK sip:gw@203.0.113.20 SIP/2.0
Via: SIP/2.0/WSS labua.invalid;branch=z9hG4bKlabws03
Max-Forwards: 70
From: "Alice" <sip:alice@example.com>;tag=labws2
To: <sip:+15551212@example.com>;tag=gw180
Call-ID: lab-ws-call@example.com
CSeq: 1 ACK
Content-Length: 0

steps.label: DTLS
steps.note: use_srtp on the media address from the answer. Independent of the WebSocket.
steps.message:
DTLS ClientHello
use_srtp
peer 203.0.113.20:19642

quiz.q: The first hop in this study flow is
quiz.why: SIP frames follow the 101.

quiz.q: INVITE on this flow is carried
quiz.why: RFC 7118 is the transport for the SIP message.

quiz.q: DTLS belongs
quiz.why: RFC 5764 keys SRTP on the media path.

quiz.q: 100 Trying means
choices: The next hop is processing the INVITE
quiz.why: Trying is SIP. It is not the DTLS handshake.

quiz.q: The Opus line in the offer uses
quiz.why: RFC 7587 requires that clock and channel count.

quiz.q: This ladder's addresses are
quiz.why: 203.0.113.0/24 is reserved for examples.

cards.back: Use the hop buttons. One caption at a time.
Open the socket before the SIP request.
SRTP keys come from DTLS, not from ACK.
Example addresses in this ladder are documentation ranges.

lab.title: Step the softphone ladder
lab.prompt: Play or step. Stop on DTLS and say which path it uses.
steps: Step to INVITE and read the proto token.
Step to DTLS and name the path.

choices: The media path named in SDP
The WebSocket as a SIP method
check.why: RFC 5764 is independent of the signaling channel.

fault.title: ACK expected to start SRTP
fault.symptom: The ACK is present and RTP arrives in the clear. The debugger says the dialog is finished so encryption should be on.
fault.log:
ACK sip:gw@203.0.113.20 SIP/2.0
CSeq: 1 ACK
no DTLS on 203.0.113.20:19642
choices: SRTP keys come from DTLS on the media path, not from ACK
ACK carries the SRTP master key
A missing ACK is what RFC 5764 uses as the key
Clear RTP is required after 200 OK
fault.why: RFC 5764 establishes SRTP keys with DTLS, independent of signaling.
fault.cause: The trace stopped at ACK and never looked at the media handshake.
fault.fix: Capture the media port from the answer and look for the DTLS handshake and use_srtp before you call the audio secure.
